I'm not sure if you're referring to the Polygon review but it had a similar complaint that there was no fanfare for solving a puzzle and the only reward was another puzzle beyond it. It's puzzle game. It rewards you with new, more complicated puzzles. If he doesn't like puzzles and doesn't think they are a reward, what the hell is he playing a puzzle game for?!

As to your question, it's slightly difficult to answer since this is an exploration game but not really a narratively driven one. Solving groups of puzzles lets you explore how part of the island works and does open up new areas. The puzzles themselves fall into two categories:

The first are introducing elements of complexity with different symbols. The symbols are not explained to you in text but through simple and increasingly complex puzzles that teach you intuitively what a symbol means. Those symbols are then combined in the more complex puzzles. That means sometimes you'll get stumped by a new symbol and have to travel to another part of the island to learn what that symbol means before returning. It's been described by a lot of reviewers as like learning a language, and it is. It's also one of the best learning curves I've seen since Portal.

The second set are how the puzzles interact with the environment, requiring you to consider the island itself as the puzzle, not just the panel in front of you. That's where a lot of the depth from. Light, shadows, shapes and sounds in the environment can all affect the solution to a panel. To interact with a movable ramp, you might be given a puzzle that has two solutions. One that has a line from low to high may tilt the ramp upward, and the inverse may tilt the ramp down. Another puzzle had a solution that looked like a set of stairs and revealed a set of stairs leading down in front of me.

Whether it's worth the price is a personal choice - but I'm stuck on that island juggling five puzzles in my head whilst in the office.
